_comment: Writes demo/demo_timeline_sprint3.json: the Sprint 3 video demo (about 3 minutes). Generated by demo/make_timeline_sprint3.py; record with REPLAY_STEP_PACE=0.35.

steps.say: User journey. 07:00 — the general manager opens ThreadPilot before walking the floor. The day is already on one screen.
RED: 8 orders overdue, assembly below its normal range for 6 days, 3 decisions waiting. Nothing here was asked for.
Every chart has an “i”: what it shows and why it is computed that way.
“Normal” = the previous 8 same weekdays: on this factory that cut false alerts from 0.67 to 0.1 a month.
The morning briefing, written at 07:00, each point with its supporting records.
09:40 — on the floor, she asks in her own words.

type.text: How is the TrendCart order doing?

steps.say: TrendCart has six active orders, so it asks instead of guessing.
ORD-005: 500 scarves at knitting, due 20 April. Each answer shows the tool calls behind it.
“Show more”: the planner’s reading, each tool with its arguments, and the records it used.
A second order in the same chat: ORD-120, 1,500 vests, 15 days overdue at assembly.
11:15 — a customer asks for 800 hoodies by the 25th.

type.text: Can we take 800 hoodies by the 25th?

steps.say: It asks the one thing that changes the answer: ready at the factory, or delivered?
An estimate with its assumptions — the queue’s finish date, the on-time chance, the bottleneck. Not a promise.
The Feasibility page runs the same simulation over the whole queue.
Our own queue finishes 30 April, after the 25th; an eligible outside workshop could make 10 April.
Core task, end to end. 14:30 — chase a stalled order, typed the way it is said on the floor.

type.text: ORD 5 hasn’t moved in a week, chase knitting

steps.say: It checks the claim against the record first — last activity 24 March, 8 days: true — then drafts to knitting.
Preview first. Nothing is sent until the manager confirms this exact draft.
Sent from the manager’s mailbox, and logged.

type.text: Remind me tmrw 10am if knitting doesn’t reply

steps.say: A conditional watch: at 10:00 tomorrow it notifies only if no reply has been recorded.
Hard case 1 — a wrong premise: ORD-029 “stuck since last week”.

type.text: Chase ord 29, stuck at washing since last wk

steps.say: The record says it moved today. It says so, and asks before writing anything.
Hard case 2 — no order ID, only a description.
Three orders match, so it lists them instead of picking one.
“The vest one” narrows that list to ORD-120 and drafts to assembly. Nothing sent.
Hard case 3 — an order that does not exist.
Not in the records — and it says so. It does not invent an order, a stage or a number.
